For procurements with an estimated value exceeding EFL Level E, complaints shall be lodged by an interested party within 15 calendar days from the date when the interested party first knew, or ought to have known, about the circumstances giving rise to the grounds for the potential dispute, whichever is earlier. For complaints relating to the contract award decision, the deadline is 15 calendar days from the day following the date on which the contract award decision is communicated to the bidders. The procurement authority may choose to increase the time period allowed for the lodging of a complaint. 11.3. For all procurements, the procurement authority may also exceptionally provide for shorter time periods for urgent and compelling reasons (e.g. when a delay in contract signature endangers life, property, or mission), to be duly justified by the procurement authority. 11.4. To ensure clarity in communication, the procurement authority and the party lodging the complaint are encouraged to verify the delivery and/or receipt of the information they share with each other with regard to complaints lodged. 12. Suspension of the Award 13. The procurement authority shall not award a contract if a complaint is lodged before the award is made, and results in a dispute. The suspension of the award shall remain in effect until the final resolution of the dispute (including up to Board of Arbitration stage, if the case), or until the party lodging the complaint confirms in writing to the procurement authority that it shall not pursue the matter further. 14. The decision to override the suspension of the award must be documented and approved by the same body or person responsible for making the award decision on behalf of the procurement authority. When needed, the procurement authority should attempt to obtain an extension of their bid/proposal validity period from the bidders. PROCUREMENT AUTHORITY LEVEL 17. The procurement authority shall establish internal procedures allowing for the expeditious treatment and resolution of complaints and disputes, without the involvement of the Committees. The procurement authority shall prioritize inexpensive, informal, procedurally simple, and effective resolution of complaints and disputes. The use of various dispute resolution techniques by the procurement authority, including third party neutrals, are acceptable methods. 18. Best Price-Quality Ratio or Best Value The contract is awarded based on a predetermined weighted assessment combining both price and technical criteria, where technical merit and financial considerations are evaluated to determine the most economically advantageous bid. Bid A formal offer to provide goods, works, or services at a stated price under specified conditions, submitted in response to an Invitation for Bids (IFB) in a competitive procurement process. In some cases, a bidder may be a non-commercial entity. Competitive Dialogue A procurement procedure whereby the procurement authority engages in discussions with selected bidders to develop one or more suitable solutions to a problem. Through dialogue, the procurement authority’s requirements and the vendors’ proposed solutions are refined and adapted before the submission of final bids/proposals. This procedure is typically employed for complex procurements where innovative solutions are required. Complaint A written demand or written assertion by a bidder or an interested bidder, related to the terms of or actions taken in connection with a procurement process. A complaint may or may not result in a disagreement and therefore a dispute that needs to be resolved. Contract A mutually binding legal relationship obligating the vendor to provide the goods, works, or services and the customer to pay for them following delivery and acceptance. Contractor A vendor that enters into a legally binding agreement with the procurement authority to provide specified goods, works, or services under agreed-upon terms and conditions. A prime contractor has a direct contractual relationship with the procurement authority and is responsible for fulling the contract’s terms, while a sub-contractor is engaged by the prime contractor to execute portions of the contract without having a direct relationship with the procurement authority. Submission A written document submitted to the Board constituting an appeal or a r ejoinder (if submitted by the appellant) or a reply or a sur rejoinder (if submitted by the respondent). Decision The final determination of the appeal . 3. TIME LIMITS 3 .1 The time limits prescribed in the ToR and the Directions: a) Refer to calendar days and shall not include the day of the event from which the period runs; b) Shall include the next working day of the Secretariat when the last day of the period is not a working day for NSPA; c) Shall be deemed to have been met, provided that the relevant party has been duly informed of the applicable deadline by the Competition Advocate, if the documents in question were received by midnight Luxembourg time on the last day of the deadline. 3.2 Appeals shall

CONFLICT OF INTEREST AND RECUSAL 4 .1 The term “conflict of interest” means any factor that may impair or reasonably give the appearance of impairing the ability of a Board member to independently and impartially decide a case assigned to him or her. 4 .2 A conflict of interest arises where a c ase assigned to a Panel involves any of the following: a) A person with whom the Member of the Board has or had a personal, fami ly , or other relationship which would prejudice the Board’s independen ce ; b) A Member of the Board previously served in another capacity, including as an adviser, counsel, expert, or witness in the assigned case ; c) Any other circumstance that would make it appear to a reasonable and impartial observer that the Board member’s participation in the resol ution of the matter would be inappropriate or that the Member of the Board would lack objectivity . 4 .3 Before accepting an allocated case in accordance with the Board’s internal case allocation system , Board members must disclose to the Secretariat and to the Plenary of the Board any circumstances likely to create, in the minds of the Parties, a reasonable doubt as to their independence or impartiality. They must also disclose without delay any such circumstances, even if widely known , that may arise a

content: create, in the minds of the Parties, a reasonable doubt as to their independence or impartiality. They must also disclose without delay any such circumstances, even if widely known , that may arise after they have accepted their assignment. 4 .4 A Member of the Board who has or appears to have a conflict of interest shall promptly recuse himself or herself from the allocated case by inform ing the President and the Secretariat without undue delay . 4 . 5 A P arty may submit a reasoned request for the recusal of a Member of the Board on the grounds of a conflict of interest to the President of the Board , who, after seeking comments from the Member concerned , shall decide on the request and shall inform the Parties of the decision in writing. Requests for recusal should be made within three (3) calendar days from the date on which the Secretariat inform s the Parties of the c omposition of the Panel. The President shall adopt his/her reasoned decision within th ree (3) calendar days from the NATO SUPPORT AND PROCUREMENT AGENCY AWARD REVIEW AND DEBARMENT BOARD Page 5 of 9 date of receipt of the request for recusal. A request for recusal of the President shall be referred to a Plenary of the Board, who shall adopt its decision by majority vote within three (3) calendar days from the date of receipt of the request for recusal in accordance with Rule 4.4.7 . 5. Each appeal shall contain: a) T he name and status of the Appellant; b) T he name of the A ppellant ’ s or authorised representative, if any; c) T he decision being chall enged , and a summary of the Appeal not exceeding two (2) pages ; d) The value of the underlying procurement procedure in accordance with Rules 4.7.1 - 4.7.3 ; e ) Any relevant complaints that the App ellant has made in accordance with the relevant provisions of the ToR, and the results thereof; f ) T he legal grounds on which the A ppeal is based; g ) A ny supporting evidence including where appropriate, statements of any supporting witnesses; h ) T he remedy being sought in accordance with Rule 4.12 of the ToR . 5 . 4 The Appeal and its annexes shall be submitted in searchable .pdf format unless otherwise instructed by the Boa

In the event of a f ailure to provide such proof within the deadline , the Appeal will not be registered and will not be t ransmitted to the Board. 5 . 6 The A ppeal shall be signed on the last page by the A ppellant or its duly authorised representative . 5 . 7 The documentation shall be legible . REPLY 6 .1 The reply and its enclosures shall be submitted in searchable .pdf format within seven ( 7 ) calendar days from the receipt of the a ppeal unless indicated otherwise by the Board . 6 .2 The reply shall be signed on the last page by NSPA’s representative . 6 .3 The reply shall not exceed 20 pages excluding the cover page and the list of annexes (A4 format, Times New Roman, font size 12, 1.5 line spacing, 2.5 cm margins) with each paragraph numbered co nsecutively . 6 .4 Failure to submit a reply within the prescribed time will not preclude the Board from rendering its decision based on the documents available . 7. REJOINDER AND SURREJOINDER 7 .1 At its discretion the Board may exceptionally decide that the Parties shall supplement their previously made arguments by way of a rejoinder and a surrejoinder . 7 .2 The Board may order the Appellant to submit a rejoinder responding to the arguments raised in the reply . content: A motion shall not exceed 5 pages excluding the cover page and the list of annexes (A4 format, Times New Roman, font size 12, 1.5 line spacing, 2.5 cm margins) , with each paragraph numbered consecutively. 8 .2 All requests to the Board for orders, directions, interim measures and other interlocutory determinations shall be made by a motion that stat es the grounds relied up on for the determination sought. Motions shall be made in writing and submitted to the Secretariat. 8 .3 Where the mot ion is contested, regarding issues of law or fact, the opposing Party may file a Response. Unless otherwise directed by the Board , a response to a motion shall be filed within three (3) calendar days from the receipt of the motion by the other Party. 8 .4 T he Board shall rule on the motion within three (3) calendar days from the receipt of the r esponse or may reserve its decision for its final decision. 8 .5 The Presiding member of the Panel , may at any time, either on an application of a Party or on its own initiative, issue any order or give any direction which appears to the Board to be appropriate for the good administration of justice . 9. Annexes are not to be used to submit additional argument s or facts that were not included in the appeal or reply . 9 .2 Parties shall limit their selection of documents to those relevant to the proceedings. In exceptional situations, s hould the interest of justice so require , then the Board , at its own discretion or upon reasoned request of a party , may decide to conduct an oral hearing via a secure videoconference. The length of the hearing will be decided by the Board and in full respect for adversarial process. 1 0 .2 When the Appellant relies on an error of fact , t he Board may re - evaluate the evidence at issue. T he Board may need to re - evaluate the evidence at hand and determine whether the facts on which the decision is based have been established based on clear and convincing evidence, and/or whether the established facts qualify as a sanctionable practice (in the case of debarment). This would require the Board to engage in a process of fact - finding. The purpose of such fact - finding by the Board would be to obtain detailed knowledge of the rel evant facts underlying a contested decision. 1 0 .3 When the Board considers that it has been sufficiently informed, it shall declare the hearing adjourned and deliberate in camera. 11. PURPOSE 1.1. The Agency operates under a public mandate that requires the highest standards of integrity and accountability and obliges NSPA to act with due diligence in all aspects of its operations. 1.2. NSPA operates under the basis of transparency, legality, and public interest. Suppliers, therefore, are expected to conform to the highest standards of integrity in all their dealings with NSPA. 1.3. The purpose of this Operating Procedure is to establish a Code of Conduct containing mandatory obligations applicable to suppliers. 2. SCOPE 2.1 This Code of Conduct applies to all suppliers doing business and bidders seeking to do business with NSPA. It sets forth minimum st

content: ntaining mandatory obligations applicable to suppliers. 2. SCOPE 2.1 This Code of Conduct applies to all suppliers doing business and bidders seeking to do business with NSPA. It sets forth minimum standards for all existing and potential suppliers, their employees, parent, subsidiary or affiliate entities, and subcontractors. 3. COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS 3.1 To be eligible for a contract award, suppliers must read and acknowledge this Code of Conduct, which shall be referenced in all NSPA Requests for Proposal, and agree that it sets the minimum standards expected of them. This Code of Conduct forms an integral part of all NSPA contracts. 3.2 Suppliers shall ensure that this Code of Conduct is communicated to their employees, parent, subsidiary, and affiliated entities as well as any subcontractors, and that it is done in a manner that is understood by all. 4. LABOUR STANDARDS 4.1 Forced or compulsory labour 4.1.1 Suppliers shall not have recourse to any use of forced, bonded, indentured labour or involuntary prison labour. 4.1.2 All work, including overtime work, shall be voluntary and workers shall be free t o leave upon reasonable notice. Suppliers shall keep a record of such payments. Deductions from wages are permitted only under condit ions and if prescribed by the applicable law, regulations, or collective agreement. Suppliers shall inform the workers concerned of such deductions. 4.2.3 The wages, hours of work and other working conditions provided by suppliers shall be not inferior to the best conditions existing locally, for work of the same character performed in the same working position and environment. 4.3 Health and Safety 4.3.1 Suppliers shall comply with all applicable legislation, regulations, and directives to ensure a safe and healthy workplace or location where production occurs and/or where services are performed. 4.3.2 At a minimum, suppliers shall ensure access to potable water and sanitary facilities; fire safety; emergency prepared

Suppliers shall also ensure these same standards apply to any dormitory or canteen facilities. 4.3.3 Suppliers shall ensure that : 4.3.3.1 the workplaces, machinery, equipment, and processes under their control are safe and without health risk; 4.3.3.2 the chemical, physical and biological substances and agents under their control are without health risk when the appropriate measures of protection are taken; and 4.3.3.3 adequate protective clothing and protective equipment are provided to prevent risk of accidents or of adverse effects to health. 4.4 Child Labour 4.4.1 Suppliers shall not employ children below the minimum age of employment or completion of compulsory schooling permitted by the applicable law where the performance, in whole or in part, of a contract takes place. 4.4.2 All workers under the age of 18 shall be protected from performing any work that is potentially hazardous or may interfere with the child’s education or that may harm the child's health physical, mental, social, spiritual, or moral development. PURPOSE 2.1 The Operating Instruction (OI) details and implements the Acquisition by Qualified Options (AQO) framework for complex acquisition programmes undertaken by the NSPA Acquisition Directorate under the NSPO Partnership framework . The OI is subordinate to R

folder: NATO Support and Procurement Agency — NSPA
content: the Acquisition by Qualified Options (AQO) framework for complex acquisition programmes undertaken by the NSPA Acquisition Directorate under the NSPO Partnership framework . The OI is subordinate to Reference A and the specific objectives of this framework are to: 2.1.1 implement the fundamental principles of fairness, openness, transparency and non - discrimination that underlie NATO and NSPO p rocurement; 2.1.2 establish a flexible, adaptable but robust framework for acquisition programmes that involve the development and acquisition of complex and/or innovative capabilities and platforms; and, 2.1.3 give acquiring Partnership Member Nations clear avenues for input and decision at appropriate points in time, hence promoting trust and cooperation between Partnership Member Nations in a complex, high - level and high - stakes acquisition programme. NATO UNCLASSIFIED NSPA OI 2200 - 01 19 June 2026 NATO UNCLASSIFIED -6- 2.2 An AQO approach promotes competition and innovation by translating the capability needs of the Partnership Member Nations into a stringent set of requirements for industry to meet. It also seeks to give industry meaningful opportunities to propose different innovative approaches, concepts or solutions to meet Partnership Member Nations’ requirements. The outcome of an AQO process is for a limited set of unique solutions to be proposed to Partnership Member Nat

folder: NATO Support and Procurement Agency — NSPA
content: tive approaches, concepts or solutions to meet Partnership Member Nations’ requirements. The outcome of an AQO process is for a limited set of unique solutions to be proposed to Partnership Member Nations, who shall be able to choose one or more solutions, based on their relative merits, following a process that provides them with the assurance that all solutions meet Partnership Member Nations’ requirements and were the result of fair, transparent and open competition. 3. SCOPE This OI is available to any complex acquisition programme or project that is part of the Acquisition Directorate, and shall apply to those programmes or projects that initiate an AQO approach. The programme or project shall also be part of a Partnership . 4. DEFINITIONS 4.1 An Acquisition Organisational Element (AOE) is an organisational group or sub - group under the Acquisition Directorate which supports the initiatives of an NSPO Support or Procurement Partnership (herein referred to as “Partnership”). AOE includes the embedded Finance and Procurement function without prejudice to the authority and responsibilities of these functions in addition to their contribution to the AOE. The AOE is responsible for undertaking the evaluation of the AQO offer(s) in accordance with the Source Selection Plan. Following completion of the evaluation process, the QOs are presented by the AOE to the Partnership Commi

Following completion of the evaluation process, the QOs are presented by the AOE to the Partnership Committee . 4.2 A Project Group is a subordinate body which has been created by decision of the Partnership Committee . A Project Group is the mechanism by which Partnership Member Nations can execute a Q ualified O ption . The participants to a Project Group are responsible, vis -à- vis the Partnership, for the costs and liabilities of the projects undertaken in the Project Group, as provided for under the Partnership Agreement (PA) . 4.3 A Qualified Option (QO) is a bid evaluated by the AOE as meeting the qualification threshold , established in the approved Source Selection Plan , reached in the course of an AQO evaluation process, declared a successful concept, design or prototype, and made available to Partnership Member Nations through a dedicated Project Group. 4.4 A Qualified Vendor is a vendor whose AQO offer(s) was assessed by the AOE as QO(s). GENERAL PRINCIPLES 5.1 An AQO may be initiated where the AOE is tasked by a Partnership Committee with the acquisition of a complex capability and where it is expected that industry can offer different approaches, concepts and solutions to problems. It gives the AOE the ability to present Partnership Member Nations with the comparative advantages and disadvantages that could not have been accurately foresee n at the Request for Proposal (RFP) stage and which can satisfy the capability and operational requirements of Partnership Member Nations. 5.2 The Director of Acquisition is responsible for oversight of AQO, without prejudice to the roles and functions of the Chief Procurement Officer as provided in OI 4200 - 01. The development of the Source Selection Plan is a Procurement led activity. 6.3.2 The Source Selection Plan shall provide for the maximum number of QOs anticipated at the end of the AQO procurement process. This number should be determined based on the assessment of the likely number of different approaches from industry, so that varyin g approaches have a chance to qualify, while not compromising the robustness or integrity of the requirement or impacting the competitive nature of the process. The number of QOs should normally not exceed five (5), with three (3) being the target. 6.3.3 The Source Selection Plan shall also clearly state whether, and under what conditions, vendors are able to submit more than one bid or to participate as a partner or sub - contractor in the bids submitted by other vendors. The requirements included in the Source Selection Plan should be final, unless the Acquisition Strategy provides for a Competitive Dialogue procedure. The requirements should be tailored in their form and content to the nature of the AQO strategy; meaning that these requirements should ensure that more than one technical or conceptual approach to the requirement is potent ially commercially viable. 6.3.5 The Source Selection Plan shall provide for the Best Value bid evaluation criteria and processes, as well as the qualification threshold(s) for application in the assessment of bids. Where applicable, the Source Selection Plan shall also provide for the methods and criteria to be used for any second level assessments/refinement of QOs. content: The purpose of this Operating Instruction is to establish a pre - contract award complaint s procedure for vendors to challenge certain decisions made by NSPA in the context of NSPA procurements. 3. SCOPE This instruction is applicable to all competitive solicitation processes up to contract award and Notifications of Planned Sole Source Award (NPSSA) concerning requirements ≥ 800K € conducted by NSPA . 4. GENERAL PRINCIPLES 4.1 The following principles shall apply to the complaint proce dure : 4.1.1 All complaints and appeals shall be made in good faith. 4.1.2 Complaints and appeals against NSPA decisions and determinations are inadmissible if the bidder was ineligible for the relevant competitive solicitation process. 4.1.3 B reaches or errors that do not materially affect the outcome of the final decision shall not lead to the annulment of said decision. 4.2 Complaints that fail to adhere to any of the principles above shall be dismiss ed as will complaints from bidders that acknowledge non - compliance with any one mandatory requirement . NATO UNCLASSIFIED NSPA OI 4200 - 08 26 June 2025 NATO UNCLASSIFIED - 6 - 5. SUBMISSION OF COMPLAINTS 5.1 Bidders may challenge NSPA decisions for one of the reasons set out i n Paragraph 5.3 below . 5.2 When submitting complaint s , bidders are precluded from correct ing , alter ing , add ing or dele ting any part of the ir bid. 5.3 Groun

PROCEDURE 6.1 Informal Dispute Resolution Be fore submitting the complaint, bidders shall make good faith effort s to resolve amicably the dispute . The start of the info rmal dispute resolution process do es not suspend the time limits for submitting a complaint unless expressly agreed to by the Competition Advocate . 6.2 Timelines The time limit s for filing complaints depend on the d ecision being contested and are provided in P aragraphs 6.2.1 – 6.2.4 b elow . In exceptional circumstances, the Competition Advocate may seek further information from subject matter experts not involved with the RFP (e.g. technical experts) . 6.5.3 The Competition Advocate shall issue a written decision, stating the ir findings and reasons for the decision, normally within 15 NSPA business days fr o m the receipt of the complaint . 6.6 Appeal Procedure before the NSPA Award Review and Debarment Board 6.6.1 T he bidder may challenge the Competition Advoc ate ’s decision , by refer ring the dispute to the NSPA Award Review and Debarment Board (ARDB) for adjudication . 6.6.2 The adjudication shall be conducted in accordance with the ARDB’s Terms of Reference (Reference E ) . 6.6.3 The decision of the ARDB shall be final. 7. REMEDIES 7.1 Remedies for Complaints for Unduly Restrictive Requirements If the complaint for unduly restrictive requirements pursuant to Paragraph 5.3.1 is we ll - founded, NSPA shall amend the RFPs by removing

folder: NATO Support and Procurement Agency — NSPA
content: 1 Remedies for Complaints for Unduly Restrictive Requirements If the complaint for unduly restrictive requirements pursuant to Paragraph 5.3.1 is we ll - founded, NSPA shall amend the RFPs by removing unduly restrictive specifications or requirements and re - advertise the RFP . NSPA may also discontinue the competitive solicitation process. 7.2 Remedies for Complaints for Determinations of Non - Compliance If the complaint for a determination of non - compliance pursuant to Paragraph 5.3.2 is well - founded, NSPA shall amend the technical evaluation report or conduct a new technical /commercial evaluation . NSPA may also discontinue the competitive solicitation process. 7.3 Remedies for Complaints Relating to Notifications of Planned Sole Source Awards If the complaint for an erroneous determination of the sole source character of a requirement pursuant to Paragraph 5.3. 3 is well - founded, NSPA shall cancel the Notification of Planned Sole Source Awards and issue a competitive RFP. NSPA may also discontinue the process. NATO UNCLASSIFIED NSPA OI 4200 - 08 26 June 2025 NATO UNCLASSIFIED - 9 - 8. INAPPLICABILITY OF REMEDIES DUE TO SECURITY CONCE R N S Notwithstanding P aragraphs 7 .1 to 7 . 3 above , if the remedies could have serious security implications, upon the recommendation of the Gener al Manager, the Competition Advocate may dismiss the complaint. This decision shall

content: .1 to 7 . 3 above , if the remedies could have serious security implications, upon the recommendation of the Gener al Manager, the Competition Advocate may dismiss the complaint. This decision shall not be subject to appeal. 9. ENTRY INTO FORCE This procedure shall enter into force on 2 6 June 2025 . From the effective date, all pre - award complaints submitted to NSPA shall be subject to this procedure. PURPOSE An independent NSPA Award Review and Debarment Board (the “Board”) is established to enhance the trust and confidence of stakeholders in NSPA dec isions regarding source selection and contract awards. The Board is also established to review debarment decisions affecting suppliers alleged to have engaged in sanctionable practices in order to ensure that resources and funds entrusted to NSPA are us ed only for their intended purposes. The Board is competent to hear and make final decisions on appeals on the grounds listed in Paragraph 4.7 below. 3. SCOPE This Operating Instruction contains the rules of procedure applicable to the Board. 4. GOVERNANCE, COMPOSITION AND OPERATION OF THE BOARD 4.1 Composition of the Board and Appointment of Members 4.1.1 The Board shall be composed of five procurement and/or legal experts external to NSPA and appointed by the General Manager (GM) through a competitive selection process. 4.1.2 All members of the Board shall be nationals of NATO Member Nations. 4.1.3 As a transitional measure, the Board may operate with a more limited composition until all five members of the Board have been appointed. 4.1.4 Once all members of the Board are appointed, they shall hold a plenary meeting with the Secretariat and agree on any procedure not provided for under these rules. The President and the Vice-President shall be elected for a two-year term that can be renewed for one additional two- year term. 4.1.6 The President of the Board shall declare the opening and closing of each plenary meeting, direct the discussions in plenary meetings, ensure observance of these rules, accord the right to speak, put questions and announce decisions. The President shall rule on points of order and, subject to these rules, shall have complete control of the proceedings at any meeting. 4.1.7 The Vice-President shall act as President where the President is unable to perform their functions. When the Vice-President, acting in replacement of the President, is also unable to perform their own functions, a new officer shall be elected. 4.1.8 NSPA shall equip the Board with a Secretariat. The Secretariat shall be tasked with providing administrative support to the Board and manage the communications between the parties. 4.2 Panel Composition and Venue 4.2.1 All appeals before the Board shall be reviewed by a three-member panel and decided by majority decision. 4.2.2 The Board shall normally hold remote sess

Where in situ meetings are required, the Secretariat of the Board may convene a meeting at NSPA or another suitable location. 4.3 Eligibility for Appointment To be eligible for appointment as a member of the Board, a person shall: 4.3.1 be of high moral character and impartial; 4.3.2 possess at least ten years of experience in the field of public law, international procurement, dispute settlement, arbitration or debarment. 4.3.3 be fluent in English (working knowledge of French is desirable). 4.4 Independence of the Board 4.4.1 A member of the Board shall be appointed for one non-renewable term of six years. 4.4.2 A member of the Board shall not be eligible for any appointment within NSPA for a period of two years following their term of office. 4.4.3 Former NSPA personnel are ineligible to apply for positions until at least two years have lapsed since their departure from NSPA. 4.4.4 Before accepting employment with any entity that has appeared before the Board within two years after separating from service, former Board members shall inform the Board’s Secretariat of their intention in writing, providing all relevant informatio

NATO UNCLASSIFIED NSPA OI 4200-09 18 December 2025 NATO UNCLASSIFIED -7- 4.4.5 A member of the Board shall serve in their personal capacity and enjoy full independence. 4.4.6 A member of the Board who has, or appears to have, a conflict of interest shall recuse themselves from the case. Where a party to the proceedings requests such recusal, the decision shall be taken by the President of the Board. 4.4.7 In the case where a party to the proceedings requests the recusal of the President of the Board, due to a conflict of interest or the appearance of it, the decision shall be taken by a majority vote of the panel members, excluding the President of the Board who shall have no voting rights. In case of equal votes, recusal of the President will prevail. 4.4.8 In case of misconduct or incapacity, a member of the Board may only be removed by the decision of the GM upon confirmation by the other members of the Board. 4.4.9 A member of the Board may resign by notifying the GM in writing. The expenses associated with the remuneration of the members of the Board in each appeal shall be borne by the appellant. 1 4.6.2 The combined fees of the Board members deciding on the Appeal in no circumstance can exceed the fees paid by the appellant. 4.6.3 Unless the required fees have been duly received from the appellant, the Secretariat sha

The appeal against debarment of suppliers must be based on one or several of the following grounds: a. NSPA breached the supplier’s procedural right s by failing to give it an opportunity to respond to allegations or by failing to take into account exculpating evidence; b. NSPA made an error of law in determi ning that the alleged conduct qualified as sanctionable practice (see Paragraph 5.1 of Reference F). 4.7.5 The Board shall not be competent to hear appeals: a. on grounds other than those listed in Paragraph 4.7.1 to Paragraph 4.7.4; b. from individuals or entities that did not participate in the competitive solicitation process or, for appeals challenging a sole source determination pursuant to Paragraph 4.7.3, from individuals or entities that did not submit evidence of their capabilities in accordance with Article 6.3 of Reference C; c. from individuals or entities that failed to submit their tender, bid or proposal before the specified closing date (unless the bidder can

PURPOSE This Operating Instruction (OI) seeks to ensure that sourcing is fully aligned with NSPA’s principles and goals. It sets forth the rules to determine a supplier's eligibility for registration in the NSPA Source File, to receive NSPA solicitations and to submit offers. The OI identifies all NSP A personnel involved in this process and the principles guiding their p erformance to ensure the goods, services and works th e Agency purchases , meet customers ’ requirements in compliance with the applicable policy and ultimately deliver value for money. 2. The most common type of e - auction is “reverse auction”. PRINCIPLES 5.1 Equality of A ccess to Public Procurement and Equal Treatment Sourcing shall be performed to allow for strict compliance with the principles of equality of ac cess to public procurement and the equal treatment of all suppliers in order to enhance the chance of a successful competitive process. 5.2 Transparency Transparency is the guiding principle to ensure that sourcing is performed on behalf of NATO with honesty , compliance and integrity. 5.3 Competition Above the low value threshold (i.e. Financial Level ‘B’), NSPA shall stimulate competition to ensure customers obtain the best solution pursuant to NSPO Procurement Regulations 4200 and the NSPA OI 4200 - 01. 5.4 Effectiveness Sourcing shall facilitate the selection of suppliers through the receipt, retention and reporting of supplier eligibility and performance information . It consolidates r egistration and performance - related information submitted by the Programme Offices and Divisions (POD) throughout the Agency. DEBARMENT Debarment is a measure that renders a supplier ineligible to participate in NSPA procurements and enter into contracts with or involving NSPA following the determination, by NSPA, that said supplier has engaged or attempted to engage in a s anctionable p ractice . 5.1 Sanctionable Practices 5.1.1 Practices that are sanctionable under this Operating Instruction include: 5.1.1.1 b reaches of section 4.1 of the NSPA Code of Conduct ; 5.1.1.2 a violation of the oblig ations contained in the NSPA Supplier Code of Conduct ; 5.1.1.3 a cts or omissions by a supplier that may hinder the inves tigations with a view to determine whether a s anctionable p ractice occurred . 5.1.2 Whether a practice is sanctionable does not depend on whether it occurred in connection with a NSPA procurement or contract. 5.2 Attribution of A cts by the Supplier ’s E mployees , A gents or R epresentatives Vendors are deemed to be vicariously liable for sanctionable acts of their employees and agents. 5.3 Cross - Debarment NSPA may implement debarment decisions made by NATO Member Nations , Partner Nations, and other NATO bodies . 5.4 Debarment D ue to a C riminal C onviction A supplier may also be debarred if it has been established by a court of law that said supplier engaged in criminal conduct, even if the conduc

Where necessary, a n investigator shall be designated to conduct an investigation . The investigator shall indicate whether the allege d s anctionable p ractice ( s ) occurred on b alance of p robabilities. Before making such a determination, the Competition Advocate shall seek advice from the NSPA/NSPO Office of the Legal Advisor , who will recommend an appropriate period of debarment . 6.3.1 If the Competition Advocate dete rmines that the allegations of s anctionable p ractice are not substantiated, they shall discon tin ue the debarment. It corresponds to the “administrative section” used in A rticle 35 of the Convention. Administrative Financial Plan (AFP) The AFP compares the Ad ministrative Maximum Financial Commitment of a Programme Decision with the total estimated administrative cost of the programme. Administrative Maximum Financial Commitment (AMFC) For definition, see Annex OMP 2 - B. Agent An entity is acting as an agent w hen it does not have exposure to the significant risks and rewards associated with the sale of goods or the rendering of services (see IG 34 of IPSAS 9 implementing guide). Aggregated Administrative Budget (AAB) Admini s trative budget created assembling the Administrative Budgets for all functional areas active in OCCAR - EA. It provides the BoS with a corporate overview of the administrative activities/costs planned/expected in a year. The A A B shows at OCCAR level the total amount of each Programme /Site/Central Office Administrative Budget. It corresponds to the “ administrative section” used in Article 35 of the Convention. al amount of each Programme /Site/Central Office Administrative Budget. It corresponds to the “ administrative section” used in Article 35 of the Convention. Aggregated Operational Budget (AOB) Operational budget created assembling the Operational Budget s for all functional areas active in OCCAR - EA. It provides the BoS with a corporate overview of the operational activities/costs planned/expected in a year. The AOB shows at OCCAR level the total amount of each Programme Operational Budget. It corresponds to the “operational section” used in Article 35 of the Convention. Borrowing The means to obtain or receive cash (or cash equivalent) on loan for use during a temporary period of time, intending to give it (or something equivalent) back to the lender. Budget Area An OCCAR organisational financial entity supported by a Programme Decision – except for Central Office and Sites - for which an administrative and/ or operational budget is established. Examples of budget areas are Central Office (AB), ProgD XYZ (AB/OB), Programme Division XYZ (AB) and (some) Sites (AB). Budget - compliant An activity is said to be “budget - compliant ” when it can be planned in a way that it does not cause the CO AB to cross the Flat Line. ause the CO AB to cross the Flat Line. Call For Funds (CFF) The CFF is the process whereby OCCAR - EA requests the Participating States to contribute an agreed amount of funding to cover the emerging liabilities. Commitment A commitment is an authorisation to make a liability for which an expenditure shall result. There are two types: legal commitment represents the liability associated to contracts or legal obligations Template IP 1 7 - 1 - 1 Issue 6 20240802_OMP 10 Financial Rules_Issue10 - Page 9 of 31 financial commitment is most often the result of legal commitment. On a yearly basis, it represents the funding liabilities associated to budgets. Contribution The Contribution is the finan cial participation granted by a Nation to OCCAR - EA. Contributi ons are transferred to OCCAR - EA in response to CFFs. Contributor Contributor is a Member State (MS), a Participating State (PS) and any other entity (Cooperating Entity, Observer) that transfers funds to OCCAR - EA as contributions to one or more of OCCAR - EA budget areas for the management of programmes . Cooperating Entity An organisation/agency that has an agreement with OCCAR to cooperate in a defined area/activity. Fina ncial Plan Administrative/Operational Financial Plans (AFP/OFP) compares the Administrative or Operational Maximum Financial Commitment of a Programme Decision with the total estimated administrative or operational costs of the programme. Financial Statem ents (FS) Financial Statements are the documents prepared according to Article 36 of the OCCAR Convention. They consist of a Section I (principal related Administrative transactions) and of a Section II for additional disclosures (agent related Programme O perational Budget transactions). Financial Strategic Aim Refer to the annual Business Plan for the list of corporate financial strategic aims. Flat Line Ceiling set to keep the growth of CO AB under control. It is calculated considering the budget of previous year and the inflation rate. It cannot be exceeded unless in specific cases foreseen in this document. Indirect costs Administrative costs which are reallocated to the Programmes Divisions (e.g. Site costs, CO PS costs) and displayed in Chapter 4 of a budget area. Investment The purchase of a good or service with a n expectation of favourable future returns in the long term. Liabilities The liabilities are the present obligations of OCCAR, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of financial resources. Member States Those States which are parties to the OCCAR Convention. Purpose This OCCAR Management Procedure (OMP) sets out the governing principles and fundamental rules under which OCCAR shall undertake its financial administration, including the financial relationship among the different contributors to OCCAR - EA budgets (Member States, Non - Member States, Cooperating Entities and

shall undertake its financial administration, including the financial relationship among the different contributors to OCCAR - EA budgets (Member States, Non - Member States, Cooperating Entities and Observers). It shall be applied to all financial activities of the organisation and adhered to by all OCCAR - EA staff. 2. Scope The principal aim of this OMP is to provide OCCAR with the financial organisation and tools that it needs to manage its programmes in the most effective way in order to successfully fulfil OCCAR’s obligations and to effectively achieve the financial strategic aims established for the Organisation. Through approval of this OMP, the Board of Supervisors (BoS) delegates financial powers to the OCCAR - EA Director (hereinafter referred to as “the Director”), Committees and Boards as set out below. 3. Int roduction 4.1 Authority This OMP is established in accordance with Chapter IX (Article 34) of the Convention. 4.2 Implementation and Administration The Director has overall responsibility for the implementation of this OMP and to ensure that it is reviewed and updated as required. By delegation of the Director, the day - to - day implementation and administration of this OMP shall be the task of the Head of Finance Divisi on ( Ho FD) who is the Senior Finance Officer 1 . The OMP is structured as a core document which outlines the principles guiding the financial management of OCCAR - EA and with the linked annexes providing details by subject areas. The BoS retain s the power to approve changes in the core document after a proposal for amendments is endorsed by the Finance Committee (FC) . The FC has the delegation to approve amendments to the annexes and to approve minor editorial amendments to the core document . These Procedures and Guidelines shall be made available to the national representatives to the FC. 4.4 Financial Year OCCAR’s F inancial Year (F Y) shall be the calendar year from 1 st January to 31 st December. 4.5 Programme Financial Activit ies Any financial activity undertaken by OCCAR - EA and relating to a programme, shall be covered by a Programme Decision (ProgD) in force which specifies financial ceilings for both administrative (AMFC – Administrative Maximum Financial Commitment ) and operational (OMFC – Operational Maximum Financial Commitment ) expenditures for its lifecycle . OCCAR - EA shall ensure that all financial activ ities relating to a ProgD are performed before its term ination . 4.6 Other Provisions For financial matters, OMP 10 shall prevail over other OMPs. BoS decisions which have financial consequences shall, if relevant, be incorporated into OMP 10. 5. Financ e Stakehol ders and Governance 5

For financial matters, OMP 10 shall prevail over other OMPs. BoS decisions which have financial consequences shall, if relevant, be incorporated into OMP 10. 5. Financ e Stakehol ders and Governance 5.1 General Organisation The financial governance of OCCAR is achieved through a coordinated effort of the following stakeholders: - Board of Supervisors (BoS) - Finance Committee (FC) - Future Task and Policy Committee (FTPC) - Programme Board (PB ) / Programme Committee (PC) - OCCAR - EA Director - Head of Finance Division (HoFD) - OCCAR Staff Members ( CO, PDs and Sites ). Refer to the OMP 1 (Princip al Programme Management Procedure) and OMP 3 ( Corporate Management/ Terms of Reference - ToR ) for the tasks and responsibilities of each stakeholder , further details and specifications focused on financial Template IP 1 7-1-1 Issue 6 20240802_OMP 10 Financial Rules_Issue10 - Page 13 of 31 governance and management are provided below in th is document and/or in the annexes . 5.1.1 Board of Supervisors The Board shall decide on all financial issues delegated to other Committee s when these cannot make a decision . 5.1.2 Finance Committee The FC is responsible for the direction of all financial matters in accordance with the ToR defined in OMP 3 and the authority delegated in this document. The FC shall monitor the operation and effectiveness of OCCAR - EA’s financial management and

nancial matters in accordance with the ToR defined in OMP 3 and the authority delegated in this document. The FC shall monitor the operation and effectiveness of OCCAR - EA’s financial management and shall advise and propose to the BoS the general policies on OCCAR financial matters. The FC has the responsibility for the approval of the AB for Central Office (CO) and for Sites in line with paragraph 7 .4 Budget Approval . 5.1.3 Future Task and Policy Committee With the support of the Finance Committee (FC), the FTPC shall monitor the integrity of the Financial Statements of OCCAR - EA. The FTPC shall also review the effectiveness of the OCCAR - EA’s internal control framework. In coordination with the FC, the FTPC may draw up specific policy that might affect financial and administrative matters. 5.1.4 Programme Board and Programme Committee The Programme Committee shall oversee the financial management of a programme. Unless otherwise specified by a Programme Board written decision, the PC is responsible for the approval of the Administrative Budget (AB) (d irect and i ndirect costs) and Operationa l Budget (OB) for the programme. 5.1.5 OCCAR - EA Director The responsibilities are according to Chapter V Article 21 of the Convention and the Director’s ToR defined in OMP 3. The Director holds overall responsibility for financial planning, budgeting, in year management and accoun

according to Chapter V Article 21 of the Convention and the Director’s ToR defined in OMP 3. The Director holds overall responsibility for financial planning, budgeting, in year management and accounting. In fulfilling his responsibilities to the BoS, the Director shall draw on the expertise of the Head of the Financ e Division. The Director is entitled to formally sub - delegate, to the fullest extent possible, authority further withi n OCCAR - EA with the aim of achieving highest performance in the financial management of OCCAR - EA. 5.1.6 Head of Finance Division The HoFD maintains the accuracy, reliability and relevancy of the financial management information produced and ensures the identifi cation of OCCAR’s financial risks. The HoFD is the primary source of financial advice Template IP 1 7-1-1 Issue 6 20240802_OMP 10 Financial Rules_Issue10 - Page 14 of 31 to the Director. The HoFD is the highest authority on behalf of the Director for maintaining the integrity for all aspects of financial management. Through Finance Divisi on, the HoFD directs and co - ordinates all financial functions, processes and procedures within OCCAR - EA. FD provides financial guidance and support to Programme Divisions (PDs) and CO Divisions. 5.1.7 OCCAR Staff Members ( CO, PDs and Si tes ) Staff Members (SM) at CO, PDs and Sites with respons ibility in the financial processes shall apply the

to Programme Divisions (PDs) and CO Divisions. 5.1.7 OCCAR Staff Members ( CO, PDs and Si tes ) Staff Members (SM) at CO, PDs and Sites with respons ibility in the financial processes shall apply the principles and rules of th is OMP and follow guidance and supervision provided by HoFD through the FD , in the cascaded IPs/IGs, with the aim of ensuring an effi cient and effective standardised financial management. The Finance functional objectives of staff members shall be assigned by the P rogramme M anager s (PM) /H eads o f D ivision (HoD) in collaboration with the HoFD and shall reflect S M roles and responsibilities , to allow for standardisation of practices in the financial domain, compliance to rules and procedures, continuous improvement, efficiency and effectiveness in the achievement of OCCAR financial objectives. 5.2 Control and Audit s The Director through the HoFD shall establish and maintain an internal control system aimed at ensuring the fair, accurate and transparent management of financial resources and financial processes. The risk of fraud, malpractices and financial misbehaviour shall be ass essed and proper controls/procedures shall be implemented aimed at mitigating those risks and at preventing wherever possible the occurrence of risk events. The accuracy and fairness of financial activities are paramount and are checked periodically by mea ns of dedicat

igating those risks and at preventing wherever possible the occurrence of risk events. The accuracy and fairness of financial activities are paramount and are checked periodically by mea ns of dedicated financial audits. Financial audits may be performed by the Board of Auditors ( BoA ) and National Auditors ( NA ) according to the provisions of the OCCAR Convention, Chapter IX (art. 36) and Chapter XIII (art. 44, 45 and 47) respectively, to the relevant ToR and to the content of this document . The internal auditors ( Internal Audit Office - IAO) can audit the financ ial processes and procedures. 5.3 Reporting on financial data Reporting requirements and reports to Committees are defined in OMP 3. They are further enriched/supplemented by the financial reports required in this document and in the Annexes aimed at meeting the information needs of s takeholders on the financial management of OCCAR – EA. Further details about content, frequency and timeline are shown at Annex OMP 1 0- A - Reporting on Financial Data . 5.3.1 Outturn Report s OCCAR - EA shall provide the relevant outturn reports to Member States and Participating States outturn r eport s for each AB / OB. The CF shall highlight for each Program me Decision, the estimated need for cash to be transferred by Participating States/Contributors to OCCAR - EA for honouring the payments expected in the year. In the preparation of the CF , the annual budget, the cash balance in the ProgD bank account and the expected payments to contractors shall be taken into account. 5.3.3 Source of Financial Information The definition and availability of a single source of financial information is assessed as an important element of the internal control that shall inform all financial activities performed in OCCAR. The single source of financial information and reporting on financial data is the Financial Management System that is the part of the ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) system devoted to the financial management . Re ports and data delivered outside of the ERP shall be used only if they comply to the system. The ERP shall always reflect the current financial status both operational and administrative of all functional areas part of OCCAR. Financial data no t recorded an d not validated in the ERP shall not be considered as official data and shall not be used for reporting purposes at Corporate level. 5.3.4 In - year Financial

Financial data no t recorded an d not validated in the ERP shall not be considered as official data and shall not be used for reporting purposes at Corporate level. 5.3.4 In - year Financial Management It is deemed necessary that the FC and the BoS maintain an up - to - date clear view on the overal l progress of the in - year financial activities. T he FC shall be informed of the status of all budgets and the HoFD shall present an in - year financial management update at each FC and BoS meeting. 6. Budgets and Financial Plans OCCAR planned expenditure for the functioning of the organisation (administrative costs) and the delivery of programme s to Natio ns (operational costs) shall be recorded in dedicated budgets prepared and approved on an annual bas is. The approved budget s for the year identify the annual ce iling for both payments and transfer of funds from Contributors to OCCAR. The preparation of the budget shall be based on an accurate estimate of the expenditures for the year. Further details about budgets and financial plans are provided in Annex OMP 1 0-B – Budgets and Financial Plans. 6.1 Administrative and Operational Budgets Administrative B udgets (AB) provide cover for administrative costs , are prepared for functional areas and are structured in chapters and Budget Line Items (BLI) to allow a better control of costs/expenditure s. Template IP 1 7-1-1

vide cover for administrative costs , are prepared for functional areas and are structured in chapters and Budget Line Items (BLI) to allow a better control of costs/expenditure s. Template IP 1 7-1-1 Issue 6 20240802_OMP 10 Financial Rules_Issue10 - Page 16 of 31 Operational B udgets (OB) provide cover for operational costs and are prepared for each Programme Division. A Programme Division may have more than one OB when supported by a ProgD. The Administrative and Operational Budget for a Programme Division shall be in accordance with the relevant Programme Decisions. The ABs for each functional area and the OBs for each Programme Decision are assembled at Corporate level, to form the Aggregated Administrative Budget (AAB) and the Aggregated Operational Budget (AOB), respectively. 6.2 Budget Preparation Budgets are prepared on an annual basis. In Y 0, the budgets for Y1 and the indicative budgets for Y2 to Y4 are prepared . The HoFD leads and coordinates the Budget Preparation Process (BPP) . 6.3 Administrative Cost Sharing As a general rule , d ifferent functional areas / ProgD s have different contributors. The specific contribution a contributor shall transfer to OCCAR to honour the budgeted annual payments is calculated using rules and sharing keys as defined in Annex OMP 10-C – Administrative Costs S haring . The sharing keys used to apportion AB costs among the PS in a P

r the budgeted annual payments is calculated using rules and sharing keys as defined in Annex OMP 10-C – Administrative Costs S haring . The sharing keys used to apportion AB costs among the PS in a Programme are agreed and established at Programme level . Sharing keys used to apportion AB costs to different Programmes and functional areas are established by HoFD/FD according to this document. If not specified differently in further parts of this document, t he costs for CO are shared among MS according to sharing keys based on the voting rights assigned to each State. 6.4 Budget Approval The BoS approves the aggregated administrative and operational Y1 budgets (AAB and AOB) of OCCAR - EA . By delegation of the BoS provided by this OMP:  Programme Boards/ Committees approve Y1 administrative and operational budget s for the respective Programmes and note the indicative budgets for the following years (Y2 to Y4) ;  The Finance Committee approves the Y1 administrative budget for CO and for those Sites recognised as functional areas and note the indicative budgets for the following years (Y2 to Y4) . 6.5 Financial Plans Annually, for each ProgD in force an Administrative Financial Plan ( A FP) and an Operational Financial Plan ( O FP) shall be produced. Introduction 1.1 General OCCAR manages a wealth of information either coming from Members States, Participant States, industries or generated within OCCAR itself. Clearly, given the nature of the Corporation’s activities, much of this information needs to be safeguarded. Even for OCCAR information which is deemed to be releasable to the public (e.g., a n OCCAR press release or OCCAR information posted on the Internet) changes to its content (loss of integrity) or denial of legitimate access (loss of availability) could result in damage t o OCCAR interests. Consequently , a ll OCCAR information requires protection to ensure its integrity and availability. 1.2 Basic Principles Classified information requir ing protection in the interest of OCCAR , its Member States or OCCAR Programme Participating States , is safeguarded by the application of appropriate security measures as detailed in OMP 11. Some OCCAR documentation , though not classified, still needs to be properly protected and distributed in such a way that only persons with a need to know can have access to it. Basic Principles and Minimum Standards of Security 1.1 General These Security Regulations lay down the basic principles and minimum standards of security to be applied by OCCAR and its Member States, so that it is assured that a common standard of protection is established for Classified Information furnished or generated in connection with OCCAR Programme activities, and uniform practices are ap plied. Such Classified Information shall be distinguished either by a national classification marking or by the marking “OCCAR” together with th e ap propriate classification level. OCCAR Member States’ Government establishments and Contractors shall protect national Classified Information furnished to them in connection with an OCCAR Programme in accordance with applicable national security laws and regulations. 1.1.1 Principles of Security in OCCAR The principal objectives of security are to maintain the confidentiality of information by: a) safeguard Classified Information from espionage, compromise or unauthorised disclosure; b) safeguard important installations housing Classified Information from sabotage and malicious wilful damage; c) in the event of failure, assess the damage caused, limit its consequences and adopt the necessary remedial measures. 1.2 Personnel Security 1.2.1 Personnel Security Clearances All persons who require access to information classified CONFIDENTIAL or SECRET shall be appropriately security cleared by the competent national security authority having jurisdiction over the individual subject or legal entity to national laws and regulations and the minimum security clearance requirements set out in this OCCAR Management Procedure ( OMP ) . In particular, the aim is to adopt recognition whenever appropriate in order to allow the re - use to the largest possible extend the work achieved by other parties . Définition et cadre juridique du SPASER Le Schéma de Promotion des Achats Publics Socialement et Ecologiquement Responsables (SPASER) a été créé par la loi n°2014-856 du 31 juillet 2014. Ce schéma détermine les objectifs de politique d’achats responsables et favorise : • L’intégration de clauses sociales visant notamment à renforcer l’intégration sociale et professionnelle des personnes en situation de handicap ou éloignés de l’emploi, • L’intégration de clauses écologiques pour réduire l’impact environnemental des achats, • La promotion d’une économie circulaire et responsable. Ce schéma a été renforcé par la loi Climat et Résilience d’août 2021 rendant obligatoire la mise en place d’indicateurs « précis, exprimés en nombre de contrats ou en valeur et publiés tous les deux ans, sur les taux réels d’achats publics relevant des catégories de l’achat socialement et écologiquement responsable parmi les achats publics réalisés par la collectivité ou l’acheteur concerné » . Enfin, le décret n°2022-767 du 2 mai 2022 (effectif au 1 er ja

ies de l’achat socialement et écologiquement responsable parmi les achats publics réalisés par la collectivité ou l’acheteur concerné » . Enfin, le décret n°2022-767 du 2 mai 2022 (effectif au 1 er janvier 2023), a lui abaissé de moitié le seuil de volume d’achat, pour concerner finalement les collectivités et les Établissements Publics Industriels et Commerciaux (EPIC) dont le volume d’achats annuels est supérieur à 50 millions d’euros. Le CNES est par conséquent pleinement concerné par l’adoption d’un SPASER en réalisant chaque année un volume d’achat de l’ordre 800 millions d’euros. B. Objectifs du SPASER pour le CNES Le SPASER du CNES a pour but de : • Renforcer la dimension sociale dans ses achats notamment en ce qui concerne l‘insertion des publics éloignés de l’emploi et de personnes en situation de handicap, la lutte contre les discriminations et la promotion de l’égalité femmes-hommes, • Favoriser la dimension environnementale des achats en ce qui concerne la lutte contre le changement climatique, la promotion de l’économie circulaire et la préservation des ressources et de la biodiversité. Il poursuit également plusieurs objectifs en interne : • Permettre au CNES de faire le bilan sur sa performance en matière d’achats responsables et identifier les leviers d’action, • Établir des orientations stratégiques de sa politique d’achats durables, • Déployer une feuille de r

le bilan sur sa performance en matière d’achats responsables et identifier les leviers d’action, • Établir des orientations stratégiques de sa politique d’achats durables, • Déployer une feuille de route structurante qui favorise l’évolution des pratiques d’achats et permettre aux acheteurs et prescripteurs techniques de poursuivre leur montée en compétence, • Impliquer toutes les parties prenantes dans sa mise en œuvre. Alignement du SPASER CNES avec les objectifs du PNAD Le Ministère de la transition écologique et de la cohésion des territoires a publié en 2022, la troisième édition du Plan National des Achats Durables (PNAD). Il donne les lignes directrices et sert de feuille de route aux acteurs publics dans la mise en place de leur politique d’achats durables. Le CNES aligne son SPASER avec les ambitions nationales portées par le PNAD et répond aux objectifs fixés dans ce document, à savoir : • D’ici 2025, 100 % des contrats notifiés au cours de l’année comprennent au moins une considération environnementale (première partie du SPASER : « vers la cible des 100% des achats intégrant une considération environnementale » ). • D’ici 2025, 30% des contrats notifiés au cours de l’année comprennent au moins une considération sociale (deuxième partie du SPASER : « vers la cible des 30% des achats intégrant une considération sociale » ). Des achats décarbonés En 2020, le CNES a réalisé son troisième Bilan des émissions de gaz à effet de serre (BEGES) 1 sur les données 2019, le premier concernant les trois scopes 2 , et s’aligne ainsi sur les objectifs de la stratégie nationale bas carbone (SNBC). Celle-ci prévoit la neutralité carbone de la France en 2050, soit une réduction des émissions de 83% par rapport à 2015. Par ailleurs, ce BEGES a permis au CNES d’identifier ses principaux postes d’émissions de gaz à effet de serre, tout scope confondu. Parmi eux, les achats se situent en première ligne avec 79% des émissions au titre du scope 3. Ainsi, les achats constituent une des priorités de la stratégie bas carbone du CNES et le SPASER vise à répondre aux objectifs fixés dans cette stratégie, à savoir : • Réduire les émissions de gaz à effet de serre du scope 3 de -33% d’ici 2030 (par rapport à 2019). • Intégrer systématiquement au moins une considération environnementale dans tous les contrats d’achat d’ici 2025. 1 Rapport BEGES 2019 CNES 2

serre du scope 3 de -33% d’ici 2030 (par rapport à 2019). • Intégrer systématiquement au moins une considération environnementale dans tous les contrats d’achat d’ici 2025. 1 Rapport BEGES 2019 CNES 2 Dans le cadre d’un bilan carbone, trois scopes (périmètres) sont étudiés. Dans le cadre de l’activité du CNES, les scopes 1 et 2 sont les périmètres les plus restreints. Le scope 1 comprend les émissions directes générées par le CNES (chauffage, véhicules…). Le scope 2 inclut les émissions indirectes associées à l’énergie : l’électricité, la consommation de chaleur et de froid. Le scope 3 est plus large, comprenant les achats, l’usage du numérique, les déplacements et les déchets. cette orientation que le CNES souhaite renforcer par son SPASER le dialogue et l’échange avec ses fournisseurs pour faciliter la compréhension des besoins respectifs et garantir un développement économique vertueux par la mise en place de produits et services de qualité. a Moyens d’action Le CNES s’engage à adopter un comportement d’exemplarité vis-à-vis de ses fournisseurs : • Dans sa démarche d’amélioration continue, le CNES émet régulièrement des enquêtes à l’attention de son écosystème industriel, • Suivi qualité de la relation fournisseurs : mise en place de bilans visant à recueillir les retours des fournisseurs et utilisateurs internes et ainsi améliorer la prestation, lever les obstacles et assurer une bonne exécution du marché en cours et des suivants, • Respect des délais de paiements. Pour répondre à cet objectif, le CNES envisage d’ici 2025 de signer la Charte Relations Fournisseurs et Achats Responsables (RFAR) et à veiller au respect de ses engagements notamment via le déploiement opérationnel de son SPASER. Le CNES souhaite d’ici 3 ans, obtenir le label « Relations Fournisseurs & Achats Responsables » attestant de sa responsabilité en matière d’achats durables. 7 Communauté d’experts, un outil d’« open innovation » piloté par le CNES ; https://www.comet-cnes.fr/ 8 Guide sur les aspects sociaux de la commande publique, 2022 9 https://marches.cnes.fr/entreprise SPA

Son élaboration a fait l’objet d’un travail collaboratif qui se poursuivra en cours de mise en œuvre. Le succès de ce schéma relève en effet de l’implication de tous les acteurs intervenant dans les processus d’achat du CNES. Dans cette optique, des actions régulières de communication interne et externe seront menées pour que le schéma soit connu et compris de tous : acheteurs, prescripteurs et opérateurs économiques. Par ailleurs, ce SPASER sera révisé au moins à mi-parcours (2025) afin de mettre à jour les moyens d’action et les indicateurs en fonction des avancées et retours d’expériences réalisées. Enfin, un Comité de Pilotage dédié à l’évaluation et au suivi des indicateurs est mis en place dans un objectif d’amélioration continue des pratiques du CNES en matière d’achats durables. A. Déploiement du SPASER Le CNES prévoit dans un premier temps de déployer son SPASER en interne via différents moyens de communication, à la fois sur son portail intranet auprès de tous ses collaborateurs mais aussi dans le cadre

S prévoit dans un premier temps de déployer son SPASER en interne via différents moyens de communication, à la fois sur son portail intranet auprès de tous ses collaborateurs mais aussi dans le cadre de conférences internes. En parallèle, le CNES envisage d’organiser différentes sensibilisations et formations auprès des salariés du CNES et plus particulièrement des ingénieurs et acheteurs, afin de les accompagner dans l’appropriation, la prise en compte et la mise en œuvre des objectifs du document. B. Promouvoir et diffuser largement le SPASER Le SPASER du CNES sera également promu et diffusé largement par communication externe auprès des parties intéressées (prestataires, fournisseurs…). Il sera également consultable sur le site internet cnes.fr. Les grandes orientations du document seront présentées au titre de son objectif 10, lors d’une conférence dédiée, prévue début 2024 et en libre accès sur le site internet des COMET du CNES (cf. nota n°7). C. Création d’un Comité de Pilotage Afin d’assurer l’efficacité du déploiement du SPASER, un comité de pilotage est mis en place pour toute sa durée de mise en œuvre. Cette instance de gouvernance transverse a pour rôle d’assurer la coordination et l’accompagnement technique des équipes chargées des achats en vue de l’atteinte des objectifs fixés. Ove lo ritenesse opportuno, l’ASI potrà partecipare come osserv atore a riunioni di lavoro poste in essere dal Contraente. Riunioni Contrattuali ASI ‐ Contraente Le Riunioni Contrattuali sono quelle previste dal Piano dei Lav ori e sono di norma:  la Riunione Iniziale  le Riunioni di Avanzamento e/o di Consegna e/o di Verifica  la Riunione Finale. Tali riunioni sono richieste dal Contraente e convocate dall’AS I e si terranno sotto la direzione dell’ASI ed alle stesse parteciperà personale dell’ASI, del Con traente, ed eventualmente i consulenti delle Parti. È facoltà dell’ASI determinare l a composizione della propria de legazione presente alle riunioni. L’effettuazione delle riunioni è condizionata dalla fornitura a ll’ASI, da parte del Contraente, della relativa documentazione descritta in Allegato Tecnico e di Gest ione, almeno 15 gi

Disposizioni in materia di economia dello spazio. La Camera dei deputati ed il Senato della Repubblica hanno approvato; IL PRESIDENTE DELLA REPUBBLICA P ROMULGA la seguente legge: T ITOLO I DISPOSIZIONI GENERALI Art. 1. Accesso allo spazio extra-atmosferico 1. La presente legge regolamenta l’accesso allo spazio extra-atmosferico da parte degli operatori, quale crocevia strategico di interessi geopolitici, economici, scientifici e militari. Promuove altresì gli investimenti nella nuova economia dello spazio al fine di accrescere la competiti- vità nazionale e di favorire la ricerca scientifica, lo svi- luppo di competenze nel settore spaziale e la valorizza- zione delle nuove tecnologie correlabili all’osservazione della Terra nell’ambito delle attività di previsione e pre- venzione dei rischi connessi con i fenomeni naturali e di origine antropica. Art. 2. Definizioni 1. Ai fini della presente legge si applicano le seguenti definizioni:

le attività di previsione e pre- venzione dei rischi connessi con i fenomeni naturali e di origine antropica. Art. 2. Definizioni 1. Ai fini della presente legge si applicano le seguenti definizioni: a) «attività spaziale»: il lancio, il rilascio, la gestione in orbita e il rientro di oggetti spaziali, compresi lo smal- timento dalle orbite terrestri e la rimozione di oggetti, i servizi in orbita, l’assemblaggio e l’utilizzo di stazioni spaziali orbitanti nonché la produzione di oggetti nello spazio extra-atmosferico e sui corpi celesti; l’esplorazio- ne, l’estrazione e l’uso delle risorse naturali dello spazio extra-atmosferico e dei corpi celesti, in conformità agli strumenti giuridici adottati a livello internazionale; il lan- cio, il volo e la permanenza, di breve o di lungo periodo, di esseri viventi nello spazio extra-atmosferico e sui corpi celesti; le attività condotte attraverso le piattaforme stra- tosferiche e i razzi sonda; ogni altra attività realizzata nel- lo spazio extra-atmosferico e sui corpi celesti da operatori cui si applica la presente legge; b) «Autorità responsabile»: il Presidente del Consi- glio dei ministri o l’Autorità politica delegata alle politi- che spaziali e aerospaziali ai sensi dell’articolo 21, com- ma 2, del decreto legislativo 4 giugno 2003, n. 128; c) «autorizzazione»: il provvedimento amministra- tivo rilasciato dall’Autorità responsabil

spaziali e aerospaziali ai sensi dell’articolo 21, com- ma 2, del decreto legislativo 4 giugno 2003, n. 128; c) «autorizzazione»: il provvedimento amministra- tivo rilasciato dall’Autorità responsabile al fine di au- torizzare l’operatore spaziale all’esercizio delle attività spaziali; d) «Agenzia»: l’Agenzia spaziale italiana, di cui al decreto legislativo 4 giugno 2003, n. 128; e) «COMINT»: il Comitato interministeriale per le politiche relative allo spazio e alla ricerca aerospaziale, di cui all’articolo 21 del decreto legislativo 4 giugno 2003, n. 128; f) «costellazione satellitare»: gruppo di satelliti adi- bito a una missione comune e gestito in modo coordinato; g) «dati di origine spaziale»: dati generati da sistemi spaziali di osservazione della Terra, dati di osservazione di altri oggetti spaziali o dello spazio e dati di emissioni elettromagnetiche provenienti da terra; h) «lancio»: attività finalizzata a collocare oggetti o a consentire la permanenza di esseri viventi nello spazio extra-atmosferico, ivi compreso il tentativo di lancio; i) «gestione in orbita»: attività di controllo effetti- vo sull’oggetto spaziale, destinato ad essere collocato in orbita, la quale inizia con la separazione dal lanciatore e ha termine con la conclusione dell’operatività dell’og- getto spaziale, con l’esecuzione delle manovre di deorbi- tazione e delle attività di passivazione dell’og

a con la separazione dal lanciatore e ha termine con la conclusione dell’operatività dell’og- getto spaziale, con l’esecuzione delle manovre di deorbi- tazione e delle attività di passivazione dell’oggetto, con la perdita del controllo sull’oggetto o con il suo rientro nell’atmosfera; l) «oggetto spaziale»: l’oggetto spaziale, ciascuno dei suoi elementi, il veicolo di lancio e ciascuno degli elementi di quest’ultimo; m) «operatore spaziale» od «operatore»: persona fi- sica o giuridica che conduce, o intende condurre, sotto la propria responsabilità, attività spaziali; n) «rientro»: attività finalizzata al rientro, compreso il tentativo di rientro, di un oggetto dallo spazio extra- atmosferico sulla Terra; o) «Stato di lancio»: lo Stato definito dall’articolo I, lettera c) , della Convenzione sulla responsabilità inter- nazionale per i danni causati da oggetti spaziali, firmata a Londra, Mosca e Washington il 29 marzo 1972, ratifi- cata e resa esecutiva ai sensi della legge 5 maggio 1976, n. 426; p) «terzo»: qualsiasi persona fisica o giuridica di- versa da quelle che partecipano all’attività spaziale. conoscenze acquisite per effetto delle at- tività di previsione di cui alla lettera r) . T ITOLO II DISPOSIZIONI IN MATERIA DI ESERCIZIO DELLE ATTIVITÀ SPAZIALI DA PARTE DI OPERATORI SPAZIALI Art. 3. Ambito di applicazione 1. Le disposizioni del presente titolo si applicano alle attività spaziali condotte da operatori di qualsiasi nazio- nalità nel territorio italiano nonché alle attività spaziali condotte da operatori nazionali al di fuori del territorio italiano. Art. 4. Obbligo di autorizzazione per l’esercizio di attività spaziali 1. Le attività spaziali di cui all’articolo 3 sono soggette ad autorizzazione. 2. L’autorizzazione può avere ad oggetto una singola attività spaziale o più attività spaziali dello stesso tipo o più attività spaziali di tipo diverso tra loro interconnesse. Nel caso di lancio di più satelliti facenti parte di una me- desima costellazione è rilasciata un’autorizzazione unica. 3. L’autorizzazione è subordinata al rimborso dei costi di istruttoria e al versamento di un contributo, determi- nato ai sensi dell’articolo 13, comma 1, lettera b) , avuto riguardo alla tipologia dei soggetti richiedenti, alle fina- lità della missione, al dimensionamento della stessa e al livello di rischio. 4. Le disposizioni dei commi 1, 2 e 3 non si applicano se l’attività spaziale è svolta sulla base di autorizzazione rilasciata da uno Stato estero, riconosciuta dallo St

tessa e al livello di rischio. 4. Le disposizioni dei commi 1, 2 e 3 non si applicano se l’attività spaziale è svolta sulla base di autorizzazione rilasciata da uno Stato estero, riconosciuta dallo Stato ita- liano in base a un trattato internazionale. 5. Fuori dei casi di cui al comma 4, l’autorizzazione di cui al comma 1 può essere sostituita dal riconoscimento dell’autorizzazione rilasciata da uno Stato estero secondo criteri equivalenti a quelli previsti dalla presente legge. Il riconoscimento è disposto, a domanda dell’operatore, dall’Autorità responsabile ed è subordinato al versamento di un contributo di importo non superiore al 50 per cento di quello determinato ai sensi del comma 3. Il procedi- mento è concluso entro sessanta giorni dalla data di pre- sentazione della domanda. 6. Le somme derivanti dai contributi di cui ai commi 3 e 5 sono versate all’entrata del bilancio dello Stato e riassegnate al Fondo di cui all’articolo 23. Art. 5. e criteri: a) sicurezza delle attività spaziali in tutte le loro fasi e i loro aspetti, dalla progettazione dell’oggetto spa- ziale e delle sue componenti alla gestione delle attività spaziali, con previsione di una specifica analisi degli impatti sulla sicurezza nonché una valutazione relativa all’inquinamento luminoso e radioelettrico prodotto dagli oggetti spaziali e alla mitigazione degli effetti dei detriti spaziali, comprese le modalità per assicurarne l’eventua- le rientro nell’atmosfera in modo sicuro e, ove possibile, controllato; b) resilienza dell’infrastruttura satellitare rispetto ai rischi informatici, fisici e di interferenza, con conseguen- te capacità di identificare e gestire gli oggetti spaziali, rilevare gli incidenti, garantire il controllo dei diritti di accesso e assicurare la protezione degli assetti, in partico- lare attraverso misure di crittografia, operazioni di back up e patch , prove tecniche e gestione degli incidenti; c) sostenibilità ambientale delle attività spaziali at- traverso la verifica dell’impronta ambientale di tutte le attività svolte durante l’intero ciclo di vita dell’oggetto spaziale, dalle fasi di progettazione, sviluppo e produzio- ne alle fasi operative e di fine vita.
